claim: Sleep disorders are debilitating features of neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: Sleep disorders are debilitating features of neuropsychiatric conditions (for a review see Wulff et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wulff et al., 2010

claim: Social stress is known to cause or exacerbate both sleep and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: social stress is known to cause or exacerbate both sleep and neuropsychiatric disorders (Meerlo et al., 1997; Meerlo et al., 2001; Germain et al., 2003; Huhman, 2006)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Both self-reported sleep disturbances and objective polysomnographic recordings are predictive of the development of stress-induced disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and anxiety.
source: Notably, both self-reported sleep disturbances and objective polysomnographic recordings are predictive of the development of stress-induced disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and anxiety (Mellman et al., 2002; Koren et al., 2002; Germain et al., 2006; Bryant et al., 2010; Sheaves et al., 2016; Ben Simon and Walker, 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The degree of resilience is highly variable between individuals for reasons that are not entirely clear.
source: The degree of resilience is highly variable between individuals for reasons that are not entirely clear (Galatzer-Levy et al., 2018; Potegal et al., 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The social-defeat model has high face, construct, and etiological validity for modeling core aspects of human pathologies.
source: This model is frequently used to model core aspects of human pathologies with high face, construct, and etiological validity (Huhman et al., 1990; Berton et al., 2006; Vialou et al., 2010; Krishnan et al., 2007; Hammamieh et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Not all socially stressed animals respond equally well—some mice are susceptible, and others are resilient to the effects of stress.
source: An important aspect of this social-defeat model is that not all socially stressed animals respond equally well—some mice are susceptible, and others are resilient to the effects of stress (Krishnan et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Multiple functionally interconnected brain regions including the nucleus accumbens, amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex have a demonstrated role in determining resilience.
source: Within this model, multiple functionally interconnected brain regions have a demonstrated role in determining resilience. These regions include the nucleus accumbens (Berton et al., 2006; Vialou et al., 2010), amygdala (Jasnow and Huhman, 2001), hippocampus (Wagner et al., 2013), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC; Hultman et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Half of mice exposed to social-defeat stress without sleep restriction were resilient (interaction ratio >1.1).
source: As expected (Krishnan et al., 2007), half of these mice were resilient (interaction ratio >1.1) to the effects of social-defeat stress (4 of 8 mice were resilient; Figure 1B and C; two susceptible—interaction ratio <1, two undefined—interaction ratio between 1.1 and 0.9)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, and citation to Krishnan et al., 2007

claim: No sleep-restricted mice were resilient to social-defeat stress.
source: In contrast to the mice without sleep restriction, no sleep-restricted mice were resilient; furthermore, all sleep-restricted mice showed decreased social interaction after social-defeat stress (Figure 1B and C; five susceptible, two undefined – interaction ratio between 1.1 and 0.9)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Sleep restriction increases susceptibility to social-defeat stress.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that sleep restriction increases susceptibility to social-defeat stress and provides evidence that sleep is necessary for resilience to social-defeat stress.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing no resilient mice in sleep-restricted group

claim: Sleep is necessary for resilience to social-defeat stress.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that sleep restriction increases susceptibility to social-defeat stress and provides evidence that sleep is necessary for resilience to social-defeat stress.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing sleep restriction eliminates resilience

claim: Differences in social interaction were not due to changes in ambulatory activity.
source: Differences in social interaction were not due to changes in ambulatory activity, as all treatment-groups showed similar levels of activity during the social-interaction testing (Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Hypothalamic-pituitary adrenal axis stress-pathways are not significantly activated by sleep restriction over a 24-hour period.
source: These findings show that hypothalamic-pituitary adrenal axis stress-pathways are not significantly activated by sleep restriction (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by fecal corticosterone measurements shown in Figure 1D (note: text references Figure 1B but should be 1D based on context)

claim: Sleep is initiated by GABAergic cells projecting from the preoptic area (POA).
source: Because sleep is initiated by GABAergic cells projecting from the preoptic area (POA), we used a designer-receptor exclusively activated by designer-drugs (DREADD) to activate these POA neurons.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge without citation in this sentence

claim: A single injection of CNO increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep for approximately 6 hr at zeitgeber time 10.
source: This was validated in a separate cohort of mice at zeitgeber time 10 (ZT, ZT 12=lights off, Figure 2C), where a single injection of CNO increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep for approximately 6 hr.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Single, daily injections of CNO across the 10-day social-defeat paradigm enhanced total sleep by 79.3±12.5 min per day over control mice.
source: Single, daily injections (administered ZT 1–2) of CNO across the 10-day social-defeat paradigm enhanced total sleep by 79.3±12.5 (mean ± SEM) min per day over control mice, (Figure 2B) including 114.6±14.2 min per day of NREM sleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Daily CNO injections increased NREM sleep by 114.6±14.2 min per day.
source: Single, daily injections (administered ZT 1–2) of CNO across the 10-day social-defeat paradigm enhanced total sleep by 79.3±12.5 (mean ± SEM) min per day over control mice, (Figure 2B) including 114.6±14.2 min per day of NREM sleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Part of the NREM increase occurred at the expense of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep; REM sleep was reduced by 31.6±4.7 min per day.
source: Part of this NREM increase occurred at the expense of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep; REM sleep was reduced by 31.6±4.7 min per day.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Mice expressing the active DREADD (increased sleep) had significantly increased interaction ratios (increased resilience) after social-defeat stress, when compared to CNO-treated control mice expressing EGFP.
source: Mice expressing the active DREADD (increased sleep) had significantly increased interaction ratios (increased resilience) after social-defeat stress, when compared to CNO-treated control mice expressing EGFP (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: All mice expressing active-DREADD (increased sleep) were resilient (interaction ratio >1.1).
source: Notably, all mice expressing active-DREADD (increased sleep) were resilient (interaction ratio >1.1), whereas only half of DREADD-control mice were resilient.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Only half of DREADD-control mice were resilient.
source: Notably, all mice expressing active-DREADD (increased sleep) were resilient (interaction ratio >1.1), whereas only half of DREADD-control mice were resilient.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Increased sleep confers resilience and has a protective influence during exposure to social-defeat stress.
source: These results provide evidence that increased sleep confers resilience and has a protective influence during exposure to social-defeat stress; supportin our hypothesis that sleep plays a determinative role in resilience to social-defeat stress.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing all DREADD+ mice were resilient

claim: Sleep plays a determinative role in resilience to social-defeat stress.
source: These results provide evidence that increased sleep confers resilience and has a protective influence during exposure to social-defeat stress; supportin our hypothesis that sleep plays a determinative role in resilience to social-defeat stress.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing sleep manipulation alters resilience

claim: Both the REM and NREM sleep of resilient mice were increased throughout the active/dark period following defeat, when compared to baseline sleep.
source: Both the REM and NREM sleep of resilient mice were increased throughout the active/dark period following defeat, when compared to baseline sleep (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Post-defeat changes in total-sleep included an increase in total sleep amount over the 24 hr period.
source: These sleep changes after defeat included an increase in total sleep amount over the 24 hr period (Figure 3D) and a reorganization of sleep from typical baseline patterns.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Most of the post-defeat changes in total-sleep occurred during the active/dark period.
source: Indeed, most of the post-defeat changes in total-sleep occurred during the active/dark period (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (note: text references Figure 2D but should be 3D based on context)

claim: Control mice exposed to novel cages over 10 days did not have reorganization of REM and NREM sleep.
source: Control mice exposed to novel cages over 10 days did not have this reorganization of REM and NREM sleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Control mice exposed to novel cages had a modest increase in NREM and REM sleep during the dark period.
source: Instead, control mice had a modest increase in NREM and REM sleep during the dark period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), showing that the effect of a novel environment on sleep was minor.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The effect of a novel environment on sleep was minor.
source: Instead, control mice had a modest increase in NREM and REM sleep during the dark period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), showing that the effect of a novel environment on sleep was minor.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of novel cage control to social defeat effects

claim: NREM slow-wave activity (power 0.5–4 Hz) and theta activity (6–10 Hz) were altered in resilient mice.
source: NREM slow-wave activity (power 0.5–4 Hz) and theta activity (6–10 Hz), were also altered in resilient mice (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: NREM slow-wave activity is a standard measure of sleep-intensity.
source: NREM slow-wave activity is a standard measure of sleep-intensity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Differences in SWA reveal underlying differences in sleep regulation between resilient and susceptible populations of mice.
source: These differences in SWA reveal underlying differences in sleep regulation between resilient and susceptible populations of mice.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing different SWA patterns

claim: Sleep is both increased and reorganized after social-defeat stress exclusively in resilient mice.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that sleep is both increased and reorganized after social-defeat stress exclusively in resilient mice and suggest that differences in sleep regulation may underlie these sleep changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Figure 3

claim: Differences in sleep regulation may underlie sleep changes after social-defeat stress.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that sleep is both increased and reorganized after social-defeat stress exclusively in resilient mice and suggest that differences in sleep regulation may underlie these sleep changes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: Sleep is homeostatically regulated, as NREM sleep amount and intensity (slow-wave activity, SWA) are proportional to the duration of prior wakefulness.
source: Sleep is homeostatically regulated, as NREM sleep amount and intensity (slow-wave activity, SWA) are proportional to the duration of prior wakefulness (Borbély et al., 1981; Dijk et al., 1987)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Prior to social-defeat stress, mice later identified as susceptible showed increased sleep-recovery after 6-hr of sleep restriction.
source: Prior to social-defeat stress, mice later identified as susceptible showed increased sleep-recovery (Figure 4B, C, top row), and increased NREM SWA (Figure 3G), after 6-hr of sleep restriction; mice later identified as resilient did not show these changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B, C

claim: Prior to social-defeat stress, mice later identified as susceptible showed increased NREM SWA after 6-hr of sleep restriction.
source: Prior to social-defeat stress, mice later identified as susceptible showed increased sleep-recovery (Figure 4B, C, top row), and increased NREM SWA (Figure 3G), after 6-hr of sleep restriction; mice later identified as resilient did not show these changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (note: text references Figure 3G but should be 4G based on context)

claim: Mice later identified as resilient did not show increased sleep-recovery or increased NREM SWA after 6-hr of sleep restriction prior to social-defeat stress.
source: Prior to social-defeat stress, mice later identified as susceptible showed increased sleep-recovery (Figure 4B, C, top row), and increased NREM SWA (Figure 3G), after 6-hr of sleep restriction; mice later identified as resilient did not show these changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Both behavioral phenotypes lost similar amounts of NREM sleep during sleep restriction.
source: This difference was not caused by the amount of sleep lost, as both behavioral phenotypes lost similar amounts of NREM sleep during sleep restriction (Figure 4C, bottom row)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, bottom row

claim: The increased recovery-response in susceptible mice remained when NREM sleep was normalized for each mouse.
source: In addition, the increased recovery-response in susceptible mice remained when NREM sleep was normalized for each mouse (to the amount of sleep lost over 6-hr and 18 hr of recovery; Figure 4C, bottom row)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, bottom row

claim: After exposure to social stress, the overall patterns in NREM-sleep and NREM SWA were similar to pre social-defeat stress values.
source: After exposure to social stress, the overall patterns in NREM-sleep and NREM SWA were similar to pre social-defeat stress values (Figure 4D and F, bottom row)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and F

claim: NREM SWA in susceptible mice was greater than resilient mice, both before and after exposure to social-defeat stress.
source: Notably, NREM SWA in susceptible mice was greater than resilient mice, both before (i.e. under baseline conditions) and after exposure to social-defeat stress (Figure 4E & F, top row)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E & F

claim: Both behavioral phenotypes showed equivalent increases in REM-sleep and total sleep after sleep restriction.
source: Both behavioral phenotypes also showed equivalent increases in REM-sleep and total sleep (Figure 4D, top row)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Sleep and sleep-regulatory changes in resilient mice are not simply caused by social-defeat stress.
source: These findings demonstrate that sleep and sleep-regulatory changes in resilient mice are not simply caused by social-defeat stress, instead, differences in sleep regulation exist prior to social-defeat stress and predict resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pre-existing differences

claim: Differences in sleep regulation exist prior to social-defeat stress and predict resilience.
source: These findings demonstrate that sleep and sleep-regulatory changes in resilient mice are not simply caused by social-defeat stress, instead, differences in sleep regulation exist prior to social-defeat stress and predict resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pre-existing differences predict outcomes

claim: Pre-existing differences in sleep regulation determine the sleep-response to social-defeat stress.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that pre-existing differences in sleep regulation determine the sleep-response to social-defeat stress; these sleep responses, in turn, determine resilience.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: Sleep responses to social-defeat stress determine resilience.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that pre-existing differences in sleep regulation determine the sleep-response to social-defeat stress; these sleep responses, in turn, determine resilience.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) is important in regulating stress resilience.
source: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; prelimbic, PrL and infralimbic, IL cortex) is important in regulating stress resilience (Vialou et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The vmPFC is sensitive to the effects of sleep restriction.
source: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; prelimbic, PrL and infralimbic, IL cortex) is important in regulating stress resilience (Vialou et al., 2014) and is also sensitive to the effects of sleep restriction (Ehlen et al., 2013; Vyazovskiy et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Mice later identified as resilient showed a significant increase in baseline LFP power density in the slow-wave range (≤5 Hz) before social-defeat stress when compared to susceptible mice.
source: When compared to susceptible mice, mice later identified as resilientshowed a significant increase in baseline LFP power density in the slow-wave range (≤5 Hz) before social-defeat stress (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The difference in baseline LFP power density was found at both major vmPFC subregions targeted by LFP-electrodes.
source: This SWA in baseline NREM sleep was found at both major vmPFC subregions targeted by our LFP-electrodes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The difference in baseline LFP power density was most prominent in the PrL cortex and also detected in the IL cortex.
source: The difference was most prominent in the PrL cortex and also detected in the IL cortex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: No power differences were found in EEG recordings between resilient and susceptible mice at baseline.
source: Notably, no power differences were found in our EEG recordings (although a trend may be present ≤2 Hz; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Local differences in NREM slow-wave activity, between susceptible and resilient mice, exist in the vmPFC before exposure to social stress and can predict resilience.
source: These findings suggest that local differences in NREM slow-wave activity, between susceptible and resilient mice, exist in the vmPFC before exposure to social stress and can predict resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pre-existing LFP differences

claim: Baseline slow wave activity in the vmPFC is preferentially enhanced in resilient animals before exposure to stress.
source: Our LFP recordings reveal that baseline slow wave activity and recovery from sleep deprivation are preferentially enhanced in the vmPFC of resilient animals—before exposure to stress (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Recovery from sleep deprivation is preferentially enhanced in the vmPFC of resilient animals before exposure to stress.
source: Our LFP recordings reveal that baseline slow wave activity and recovery from sleep deprivation are preferentially enhanced in the vmPFC of resilient animals—before exposure to stress (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Wave incidence after sleep restriction, a marker of waking sleep pressure, is significantly increased in resilient mice.
source: Wave incidence after sleep restriction, a marker of waking sleep pressure, is also significantly increased in resilient mice (Figure 5C–F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–F

claim: The enhanced buildup of sleep pressure and increased homeostatic response led to faster recovery from sleep restriction in the vmPFC of resilient mice.
source: Together, the enhanced buildup of sleep pressure and increased homeostatic response led to faster recovery from sleep restriction in the vmPFC of resilient mice, thus supporting the hypothesis that NREM-related changes in vmPFC are associated with resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: NREM-related changes in vmPFC are associated with resilience.
source: Together, the enhanced buildup of sleep pressure and increased homeostatic response led to faster recovery from sleep restriction in the vmPFC of resilient mice, thus supporting the hypothesis that NREM-related changes in vmPFC are associated with resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: The POA has a well-established role in the promotion of sleep.
source: The POA has a well-established role in the promotion of sleep and multiple cell groups and neuronal subtypes within this region are involved in initiating sleep (Sherin et al., 1996; Liou et al., 1990; Chung et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Multiple cell groups and neuronal subtypes within the POA are involved in initiating sleep.
source: The POA has a well-established role in the promotion of sleep and multiple cell groups and neuronal subtypes within this region are involved in initiating sleep (Sherin et al., 1996; Liou et al., 1990; Chung et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Other physiological responses regulated by the POA include exploratory and sexual behavior, shivering thermogenesis and body temperature.
source: Other physiological responses are also regulated by the POA including exploratory and sexual behavior, shivering thermogenesis and body temperature (Conceição et al., 2019; Tsuneoka and Funato, 2021; Kroeger et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A recent chemogenetic study activated galanin-expressing neurons in the POA and reported increased NREM and decreased REM sleep, and a decrease in body temperature.
source: A recent chemogenetic study activated galanin-expressing neurons in the POA and reported findings similar to those reported here (increased NREM and decreased REM sleep), and a decrease in body temperature (Kroeger et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: All mice in the DREADD study expressed DREADD in regions of the POA known to initiate sleep.
source: All mice in the study expressed DREADD in regions of the POA known to initiate sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and all responded with increased NREM sleep (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: All mice expressing DREADD in the POA responded with increased NREM sleep.
source: All mice in the study expressed DREADD in regions of the POA known to initiate sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and all responded with increased NREM sleep (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Sleep restriction has the opposite effect of POA activation on resilience.
source: Nevertheless, when considered in the context of our other results, especially our finding that sleep restriction decreases resilience (i.e. sleep restriction has the opposite effect of POA activation), our studies provide strong evidence that changes in sleep mediate the changes we observed in resilience.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of sleep restriction and POA activation experiments

claim: Changes in sleep mediate the changes observed in resilience.
source: Nevertheless, when considered in the context of our other results, especially our finding that sleep restriction decreases resilience (i.e. sleep restriction has the opposite effect of POA activation), our studies provide strong evidence that changes in sleep mediate the changes we observed in resilience.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing sleep manipulation alters resilience

claim: Sleep regulation in the cortex is known to occur at a local level.
source: Sleep regulation in the cortex is known to occur at a local level (Vyazovskiy et al., 2011; Steriade et al., 2001; Miyamoto et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Areas that are more active during awake periods are known to have increased sleep intensity during subsequent sleep episodes.
source: areas that are more active during awake periods are known to have increased sleep intensity during subsequent sleep episodes (Pigarev et al., 1997; Dang-Vu, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Phase-coherence in the IL cortex (0.5–4 Hz, with the epidural EEG) was significantly and positively correlated with social-interaction ratios.
source: Phase-coherence in the IL cortex (0.5–4 Hz, with the epidural EEG) was significantly and positively correlated with social-interaction ratios (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: The positive correlation between IL cortex phase-coherence and social-interaction ratios increased after sleep restriction and persisted after social stress.
source: This positive correlation increased after sleep restriction and persisted after social stress.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: No positive correlation between phase-coherence and social-interaction ratios was found in the PrL cortex.
source: No such positive correlation was found in the PrL cortex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Increased phase-coherence suggests an increase in functional connectivity between the IL cortex with the global EEG (in NREM frequency ranges).
source: Increased phase-coherence suggests an increase in functional connectivity between the IL cortex with the global EEG (in NREM frequency ranges) and suggests that this increased functional connectivity between these brain regions predicts resilience.
evidence: Inferred from phase-coherence data

claim: Increased functional connectivity between the IL cortex and global EEG predicts resilience.
source: Increased phase-coherence suggests an increase in functional connectivity between the IL cortex with the global EEG (in NREM frequency ranges) and suggests that this increased functional connectivity between these brain regions predicts resilience.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between phase-coherence and social interaction ratios

claim: Phase coherence does not indicate directionality of functional connectivity.
source: Phase coherence does not indicate directionality of this functional connectivity; however, it does provide evidence that local differences in sleep are correlated with maladaptive behavioral responses to stress.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the phase coherence measure

claim: Local differences in sleep are correlated with maladaptive behavioral responses to stress.
source: Phase coherence does not indicate directionality of this functional connectivity; however, it does provide evidence that local differences in sleep are correlated with maladaptive behavioral responses to stress.
evidence: Inferred from phase coherence data

claim: Resilient animals had enhanced SWA (0.5–4 Hz range) in the PrL cortex.
source: Other subregional differences included enhanced SWA (5 A, 0.5–4 Hz range) and slow-wave-energy recovery (Figure 5B) in the PrL cortex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Resilient animals had enhanced slow-wave-energy recovery in the PrL cortex.
source: Other subregional differences included enhanced SWA (5 A, 0.5–4 Hz range) and slow-wave-energy recovery (Figure 5B) in the PrL cortex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Sleep-regulatory differences predicting resilience can be further localized to specific subregions of the vmPFC.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the sleep-regulatory differences predicting resilience can be further localized to specific subregions of the vmPFC.
evidence: Inferred from differences between IL and PrL cortex

claim: Both the IL and PrL cortex have a demonstrated importance in resilience to social-defeat stress.
source: Both the IL and PrL cortex have a demonstrated importance in resilience to social-defeat stress (Vialou et al., 2014; Lehmann and Herkenham, 2011; Covington et al., 2010; Dulka et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There is a clear positive correlation between NREM sleep in the vmPFC and resilience.
source: Nevertheless, the data demonstrate a clear positive correlation between NREM sleep in the vmPFC and resilience.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: NREM sleep plays a major role in mediating resilience to social-defeat stress.
source: Our findings indicate a major role for NREM sleep in mediating resilience to social-defeat stress based on several lines of evidence.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results

claim: Sleep deprivation decreased both NREM and REM sleep.
source: First, our sleep deprivation paradigm decreased both NREM and REM sleep, whereas activation of the POA preferentially increased NREM sleep while REM sleep was reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Activation of the POA preferentially increased NREM sleep while REM sleep was reduced.
source: First, our sleep deprivation paradigm decreased both NREM and REM sleep, whereas activation of the POA preferentially increased NREM sleep while REM sleep was reduced.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: REM sleep is unlikely to have large effects on resilience.
source: Because REM was decreased in both conditions, with opposite effects on social interaction, REM sleep is unlikely to have large effects on resilience.
evidence: Inferred from opposite effects on resilience despite both conditions decreasing REM

claim: Evidence of altered NREM sleep regulation was most prominent in the vmPFC of resilient mice.
source: Furthermore, evidence of altered NREM sleep regulation was most prominent in the vmPFC of resilient mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The frequency bands that predominate in NREM sleep were significantly higher in the vmPFC of resilient mice.
source: In this area, the frequency bands that predominate in NREM sleep were significantly higher and NREM responses to sleep deprivation were significantly enhanced in resilient mice (Figures 5 and 6)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: NREM responses to sleep deprivation were significantly enhanced in resilient mice in the vmPFC.
source: In this area, the frequency bands that predominate in NREM sleep were significantly higher and NREM responses to sleep deprivation were significantly enhanced in resilient mice (Figures 5 and 6)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: The findings strongly implicate NREM sleep in mediating changes in resilience, but do not rule out the involvement of REM sleep.
source: Together, these findings strongly implicate NREM sleep in mediating changes in resilience, but do not rule out the involvement of REM sleep.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results

claim: The effects of stress on behavior, and sleep-responses to stress, vary with sex.
source: The effects of stress on behavior, and sleep-responses to stress, vary with sex (Paul et al., 2009; Paul et al., 2006; Yohn et al., 2019b)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: It is not possible to predict how the findings relate to females.
source: The effects of stress on behavior, and sleep-responses to stress, vary with sex (Paul et al., 2009; Paul et al., 2006; Yohn et al., 2019b) thus, it is not possible to predict how our findings relate to females.
evidence: Stated as a limitation due to sex differences

claim: Female mice are not territorial.
source: Female mice are not territorial; therefore, social-defeat stress in females requires alternative defeat-paradigms.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Social-defeat stress in females requires alternative defeat-paradigms.
source: Female mice are not territorial; therefore, social-defeat stress in females requires alternative defeat-paradigms.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that female mice are not territorial

claim: Female-defeat paradigms were only recently developed and reported.
source: These female-defeat paradigms were only recently developed and reported (Yohn et al., 2019b; Yohn et al., 2019a), which prevented us from considering sex as a biological variable in the present study.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: Sleep is an active response to social stress that serves to promote resilience.
source: The present studies show that sleep is an active response to social stress that serves to promote resilience, thus demonstrating a clear causal link between insufficient sleep and maladaptive behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing sleep manipulation alters resilience

claim: There is a clear causal link between insufficient sleep and maladaptive behaviors.
source: The present studies show that sleep is an active response to social stress that serves to promote resilience, thus demonstrating a clear causal link between insufficient sleep and maladaptive behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing sleep restriction increases susceptibility

claim: Findings in the vmPFC reveal local changes in sleep that may not be visible in the global EEG.
source: Further, our findings in the vmPFC reveal local changes in sleep that may not be visible in the global EEG.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing LFP differences not seen in EEG

claim: The induced sleep response is dependent on inter-individual variability in sleep regulation.
source: This induced sleep response is dependent on inter-individual variability in sleep regulation and, if sufficient sleep is obtained, likely serves to mitigate the well-established negative effects of sleep loss on CNS function—including cognition and emotion (Krause et al., 2017; Ritland et al., 2019; Simonelli et al., 2019)
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing different sleep responses between individuals

claim: If sufficient sleep is obtained, the induced sleep response likely serves to mitigate the well-established negative effects of sleep loss on CNS function—including cognition and emotion.
source: This induced sleep response is dependent on inter-individual variability in sleep regulation and, if sufficient sleep is obtained, likely serves to mitigate the well-established negative effects of sleep loss on CNS function—including cognition and emotion (Krause et al., 2017; Ritland et al., 2019; Simonelli et al., 2019)
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research on sleep loss effects

claim: Sleep loss has well-established negative effects on CNS function—including cognition and emotion.
